GLO Record of the Week for March 29, 2021
In celebration of Women's History Month, the General Land Office team takes a journey from Wisconsin to New Mexico along the path of one of the most iconic female painters of the 20th century, known as the "Mother of American Modernism," Georgia O’Keeffe.

### Early Beginnings
Georgia Totto O'Keeffe was born November 15, 1887, on a farm near Sun Prairie, Wisconsin. Her father, Francis Calixtus O'Keeffe was of Irish heritage, and her mother, Ida Totto was of Dutch and Hungarian descent.
O'Keeffe's paternal grandfather, Pierce, immigrated to the United States from Ireland and eventually settled in Dane County, Wisconsin. Through land records available on the GLO website, we can view copies of the original land patents granted to Pierce near Sun Prairie. The patent shown on the right was a cash entry patent for 240 acres and dated January 1, 1850.
Georgia's love for art was encouraged at an early age and her interest in becoming an artist blossomed while in Wisconsin. She and two of her sisters received art lessons from a local female watercolorist, Sara Mann. Each week, the trio would travel seven miles roundtrip to downtown Sun Prairie to learn to draw and paint.
Examples of earliest known work:

### A Move East
Georgia and her family moved from Wisconsin to Williamsburg, Virginia, around 1902. Her parents reportedly placed a significant value on female education and after completing her high school studies, Georgia attended the School of the Art Institute of Chicago from 1905 to 1906.
Pictured left: "Untitled (Vase of Flowers),_"_ watercolor on paper, 1903-1905
Additional work examples:
Georgia continued to refine her craft and in 1907 she furthered her studies at the Art Student League in New York City. Her 1908 painting titled "Dead Rabbit and Copper Pot _"_(pictured left)landed her a coveted spot at League's Outdoor School in Lake George, New York _._
Over the next several years, Georgia continued her studies and took on roles as a commercial artist and also as an art teacher in various locations including Illinois, New York, Virginia, Texas, and South Carolina.

### Becoming an Icon
Georgia's first solo exhibit was shown in New York City in 1917 and she subsequently moved to the city in 1918. In New York, Georgia found herself in the midst of the male-dominated modern art movement and by the mid-1920s she became one of the movement's most famous and in-demand artists.
During this time, she experimented with perspective and many of her well-known subject matters, such as close-up views of flowers and the city's skyscrapers.
Pictured right,Georgia O'Keeffe's "Series 1, No. 8," oil on canvas, 1919.

### New Mexico and the Later Years
In 1929, Georgia visited a ranch near Taos, New Mexico where she developed a love for the state's rich landscapes and beautiful deserts. She returned every summer to create works of art.
Georgia continued to create during the 1930s and 1940s and she was even honored with two distinguished retrospectives. In 1946, the Museum of Modern Art honored O'Keeffe with their first-ever retrospective of work by a woman.
Works from her many years in New Mexico often feature the bones of animals that she collected, architecture, and vibrant landscapes.
In 1949, Georgia permanently moved to New Mexico and she purchased two properties near Taos, including her magnificent Ghost Ranch, which is open for visitors today.
Georgia lived in her beloved New Mexico for the rest of her life and continued to create, even as she suffered from a loss of eyesight. Her legacy is one of imagination, tenacity, and inspiration that paved the way for many others to come.

The patent shown on the right was a cash entry patent for 240 acres and dated January 1, 1850.
Georgia's love for art was encouraged at an early age and her interest in becoming an artist blossomed while in Wisconsin. She and two of her sisters received art lessons from a local female watercolorist, Sara Mann. Each week, the trio would travel seven miles roundtrip to downtown Sun Prairie to learn to draw and paint.
Examples of earliest known work:

### A Move East
Georgia and her family moved from Wisconsin to Williamsburg, Virginia, around 1902. Her parents reportedly placed a significant value on female education and after completing her high school studies, Georgia attended the School of the Art Institute of Chicago from 1905 to 1906.
Pictured left: "Untitled (Vase of Flowers),_"_ watercolor on paper, 1903-1905
Additional work examples:
Georgia continued to refine her craft and in 1907 she furthered her studies at the Art Student League in New York City. Her 1908 painting titled "Dead Rabbit and Copper Pot _"_(pictured left)landed her a coveted spot at League's Outdoor School in Lake George, New York _._
Over the next several years, Georgia continued her studies and took on roles as a commercial artist and also as an art teacher in various locations including Illinois, New York, Virginia, Texas, and South Carolina.

### Becoming an Icon
Georgia's first solo exhibit was shown in New York City in 1917 and she subsequently moved to the city in 1918. In New York, Georgia found herself in the midst of the male-dominated modern art movement and by the mid-1920s she became one of the movement's most famous and in-demand artists.
During this time, she experimented with perspective and many of her well-known subject matters, such as close-up views of flowers and the city's skyscrapers.
Pictured right,Georgia O'Keeffe's "Series 1, No. 8," oil on canvas, 1919.

### New Mexico and the Later Years
In 1929, Georgia visited a ranch near Taos, New Mexico where she developed a love for the state's rich landscapes and beautiful deserts. She returned every summer to create works of art.
Georgia continued to create during the 1930s and 1940s and she was even honored with two distinguished retrospectives. In 1946, the Museum of Modern Art honored O'Keeffe with their first-ever retrospective of work by a woman.
Works from her many years in New Mexico often feature the bones of animals that she collected, architecture, and vibrant landscapes.
In 1949, Georgia permanently moved to New Mexico and she purchased two properties near Taos, including her magnificent Ghost Ranch, which is open for visitors today.
Georgia lived in her beloved New Mexico for the rest of her life and continued to create, even as she suffered from a loss of eyesight. Her legacy is one of imagination, tenacity, and inspiration that paved the way for many others to come.

Based on my research, the only Georgia O'Keeffe work at the Art Institute of Chicago that meets all three criteria (New Mexico landscape, oil painting, created before 1940) is:

## **Black Cross, New Mexico (1929)**

**Details:**
- **Date:** 1929
- **Medium:** Oil on canvas (99.1 × 76.2 cm / 39 × 30 inches)
- **Subject:** Depicts a black Penitente cross silhouetted against distant New Mexico hills/mountains
- **Provenance:** Sold to the Art Institute of Chicago in 1943 (accession no. 1943.95)
- **Description:** The painting shows a thick-armed wooden cross with round nail heads in the foreground, set against densely packed gray and brown hills leading to a horizon lined with burnt orange and vivid yellow tones, topped by blue sky with hints of yellow and white suggesting moon or star

This work was created during O'Keeffe's first extended visit to New Mexico in 1929 when she visited Mabel Dodge Luhan's ranch near Taos. She painted several variations of the cross that evening, and this is her most famous composition from that series, capturing both the literal landscape and the spiritual significance of the crosses used by the Penitentes religious group in the region.

Other Georgia O'Keeffe New Mexico works in the AIC collection include:
- **Cow's Skull with Calico Roses (1931)** - but this is primarily a skull/still life, not a landscape
- Various later works (post-1940) such as *Sky Above Clouds IV* (1965)

Without access to the current full database of the Art Institute's online collection, **Black Cross, New Mexico (1929)** appears to be the sole work definitively meeting all three specified criteria.
